signals.text: For students under 16, this is further supported by a requirement to choose at least one course in each of the following broad areas of study: Humanities, Art, Music & Drama, Science, Maths, Health & Movement and English.

signals.text: At Brockwood, we offer a wide variety of subjects that can be studied at A Level, covering a substantial range of sciences, arts, and humanities subjects.
Time and care is taken to ensure that each timetable is balanced, so that students are challenged and exposed to new areas of learning, whilst developing their strengths and interests.

signals.text: From personal introductions to an exciting range of institutions and experts, to writing transcripts and references, students can arrange one-to-one meetings each week of the school year and discuss their progress or explore their options and motivations.

signals.text: Furthermore, all our youngest first-year students participate in the Health & Movement course, which provides ample theoretical and practical learning opportunities on issues of health and physical education, including lessons about sexual health, drug awareness, sleep, stress and nutrition.
Computers and Phones Brockwood recognises the incredible opportunities new technologies, such as smartphones and applications available on personal computers, provide for learning and education.
In line with this, all students are expected to maintain a vegetarian diet throughout the term time, including on school related trips and activities, and weekend visits to local towns.
Clubs and Activities In the late afternoons and evenings and on weekends, students can participate in clubs and activities, often led and organised by the students themselves.

Students can join clubs and activities, which include dance, yoga, drama, band-rehearsals, sports and indoor games, or simply read, chat, do homework, or go for a walk in the beautiful surrounding countryside.

signals.pageTitle: About Brockwood Park School - Brockwood Park School

signals.text: The strength of the community at Brockwood, developed through living and working together in a small school, means that students become effective listeners and cultivate a tolerance and maturity that will serve them throughout life.
The central concern of Brockwood has been to what degree could a community of staff and students, living and learning together, free themselves from the background of destructive conditioning?
